meta.title: Who really said "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Lao Tzu — Tao Te Ching, chapter 64. But the Chinese says a thousand li, and that it begins beneath one’s feet.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and from Tao Te Ching chapter 64. The wording is modernised: a thousand li, not miles, and “beneath one’s feet”.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: Traditionally 6th century BC · the figure to whom the Tao Te Ching is ascribed
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence closes the second paragraph of chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching, and it reads in Chinese 千里之行，始於足下. James Legge’s 1891 translation ↗ gives it as “the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step”. Two things drifted on the way to the version people quote. A li is not a mile — it is roughly a third of one — so “a thousand miles” triples the distance Laozi wrote. And the Chinese 始於足下 says the journey begins beneath one’s feet; “with a single step” is already Legge’s interpretation of that. The thought is his, the source is certain, and the English is a century of polishing.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Tao Te Ching (Dao De Jing), chapter 64
千里之行，始於足下 — qiān lǐ zhī xíng shǐ yú zú xià
A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one’s feet
James Legge, 1891 — Sacred Books of the East, vol. 39, pp. 107–108
Not securely datable; traditionally 6th century BC, linguistically argued as late as the 4th century BC

source.excerpt: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
trail: The Chinese text was read directly: Chinese Wikisource’s Wang Bi recension of the 道德經 ↗ carries chapter 64 as “九層之臺，起於累土；千里之行，始於足下” — the tower of nine storeys from a heap of earth, then the thousand-li journey from beneath the feet.

The English shown here is Legge’s. Project Gutenberg’s text of The Tao Teh King ↗ gives chapter 64 paragraph 2 ending “the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step”. The same sentence appears in the Internet Archive’s scan of the 1891 original ↗, whose catalogue record gives the publisher as the Clarendon Press, Oxford, and the date as 1891.

Wikiquote’s Laozi page ↗ files the line under Chapter 64 with the Chinese, the pinyin and the gloss “A journey of a thousand li starts with a single step”, lists the “miles” forms as variant translations, and adds that the saying is “often misattributed to Confucius”.

Wikipedia’s article on the saying ↗ states the literal meaning as “A journey of a thousand li starts beneath one’s feet” and notes the alternative English renderings “begins from under the feet” and “begins where one stands”.
source.excerptNote: Legge’s 1891 wording, transcribed from the Project Gutenberg text of his translation ↗ and checked against the scanned 1891 Clarendon Press volume ↗, where the clause falls across pages 107 and 108. The parentheses and the italic li are Legge’s own. Note that the famous sentence is the third in a series of three — the sprout, the heap of earth, then the journey — which is how the chapter builds its point.

sourceLink.text: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (Project Gutenberg)

source.rightsNote: Public domain, on both counts. The Chinese original is ancient. The English shown is James Legge’s translation, first published in 1891 by the Clarendon Press at Oxford as volume 39 of the Sacred Books of the East — four decades before the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, and Legge himself died in 1897. Quote it freely. One caution: the exact sentence most people reproduce (“a thousand miles… begins with a single step”) is not Legge’s and is not traceable to any one pre-1931 edition, so if you need a citable text, use Legge’s wording rather than the popular one.

author.name: Lao Tzu
author.heading: About Lao Tzu
author.metaLine: Traditionally 6th century BC · Chinese philosopher, ascribed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (also Laozi, 老子, “the old master”) is the figure to whom the Tao Te Ching is traditionally ascribed, and the founding name of Taoism. Traditional accounts put him in the 6th century BC state of Chu and make him keeper of the archives at the Zhou royal court, where legend has him meeting a younger Confucius. Modern scholarship is genuinely split: some historians treat him as largely or wholly legendary, others think a historical figure called Lao Dan plausible, and the dating of the text is argued separately from the dating of the man — linguistic analysis has placed the received Tao Te Ching as late as the 4th century BC.

misattribution.heading: What to watch for
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound, so nothing here refutes Lao Tzu. Two things are nonetheless worth knowing: the saying is regularly pinned on the wrong Chinese philosopher, and the English everyone quotes has drifted twice from what the Chinese says.

items.scope: Who it gets credited to instead
items.why: Wikiquote records the line as “often misattributed to Confucius” ↗. It is a Taoist sentence from the Tao Te Ching, not a Confucian one from the Analects; the two men are routinely swapped in English-language quote collections because both read as “ancient Chinese sage”.

items.who: “miles” standing in for 千里 (a thousand li)
items.why: The Chinese is 千里 — a thousand li. A li “has varied considerably over time but was usually about one third of an English mile” ↗, so the English version silently inflates the distance to roughly three times what the text says. Wikiquote lists the “miles” forms as variant translations ↗, not as the reading.

items.who: “begins with a single step” for 始於足下
items.why: 始於足下 says the journey begins beneath one’s feet — the emphasis is on where you already are, not on the act of stepping. Wikipedia gives the literal sense as “starts beneath one’s feet” ↗. “A single step” is Legge’s 1891 gloss, which then hardened into the quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: So: genuinely Lao Tzu, genuinely chapter 64, and documented in a public-domain translation you can read in full ↗ — but the memorable English is a translator’s sentence as much as a philosopher’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Chapter 64 is about acting early and acting small. The three images run in order — the arm-filling tree that was once a sprout, the nine-storey tower that was once a heap of earth, the thousand-li journey that began underfoot — and they are not motivational posters. They are an argument that large outcomes are already decided by small, unglamorous beginnings, which is why the chapter’s advice is to deal with things before they become things.

The modern reading has quietly reversed the emphasis. “Begins with a single step” is a call to action: take the step. “Begins beneath one’s feet” is closer to an observation about location: the journey is not elsewhere, it is where you are standing. The first is a slogan, the second is Taoism.
detailsBody: Who wrote it is a separate question from whether the line is in the book, and the honest answer is that the line is certainly in the book and the author is traditional. Wikipedia summarises the scholarship ↗: “Modern scholars remain divided over his identity, dates, and precise relationship to the received text: some regard the traditional Laozi as largely or wholly legendary, while others consider a historical Lao Dan plausible.” Traditional accounts place him in the 6th century BC state of Chu and describe him as keeper of the archives at the Zhou court; linguistic dating of the text itself has been argued as late as the 4th century BC. This page credits Lao Tzu because that is who the Tao Te Ching is ascribed to, not because a biography has been verified.

If you want a citable text, Legge’s is the one to use and it is free: the Clarendon Press published it in 1891 in the Sacred Books of the East, and both the scan and a clean transcription are linked above. Chapter 64 is short, and the sentence makes much more sense read with the sprout and the heap of earth in front of it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Legge's 1891 translation of Tao Te Ching chapter 64 reads: 'The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.'
The Chinese original of chapter 64 reads 九層之臺，起於累土；千里之行，始於足下 (the thousand-li journey begins beneath the feet).

The 1891 Clarendon Press edition (Sacred Books of the East 39) carries 'the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step' in chapter 64, across pages 107-108; the catalogue record gives publisher Oxford, The Clarendon Press and date 1891.

Wikiquote's Laozi page files the line under Chapter 64 with the Chinese and pinyin, translates it 'A journey of a thousand li starts with a single step', lists 'miles' forms as variant translations, and states it is often misattributed to Confucius.

Wikipedia gives the literal meaning as 'A journey of a thousand li starts beneath one's feet', identifies chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching as the source, and notes the renderings 'begins from under the feet' and 'begins where one stands'.

Modern scholars are divided over Laozi's identity and dates, some regarding him as largely or wholly legendary; traditional accounts place him in the 6th century BC state of Chu as keeper of the Zhou archives, and linguistic dating of the text has been argued as late as the 4th century BC.
Wikipedia's Li (unit) article states the li 'has varied considerably over time but was usually about one third of an English mile and now has a standardized length of a half-kilometer'.
